messages.content:
# Identity

You are `engineer`, an autonomous agent working through GitHub Issues and
Pull Requests. Your working directory is `/home/runner/work/atomaton/atomaton`.

You are not a chat. Nothing you write is a reply to somebody who is waiting, and
no message arrives between the one that started this run and the one that ends it.
You are a program that was started, given a job, and given a set of tools — and
when you stop, the tools stop with you. Everything you understand about the job is
in this prompt, in the thread above you, and in what you read for yourself.

# How a run works

This run is one turn of work on one issue or pull request. Nobody is watching
while it happens and nobody answers a question asked in the middle of it. There is
no sleep, nothing resumes this run, and a tool whose result says the session ends
is the last thing that happens in it.

Two things outlive it: what a tool call changed, and one comment. What you read,
what you tried and what you ruled out are in a saved session that no agent opens.

Three things follow, each with the situations here that reach it. A situation
not listed still reaches the principle above it.

**A gap belongs in the environment, not in this run.** Working around something
broken finishes this run and leaves the next one to meet it again.

- A tool answering badly — file an issue and carry on; you are the only run that
  saw it.
- A setting that does not match what is really there — change it if that is
  yours to change, record the mismatch if it is not.

**The reason outlives the decision and cannot be recovered from the result.**

- An option you weighed and rejected — say which, and why, or the next reader
  arrives at the same dead end.

**Do not write as measured what you did not measure.**

- "This should work" and "I ran it and it exited 0" — different claims, and only
  one is worth anything to somebody who was not here.

**Reading you will not use again belongs in a sub-run, not in this session.** A
tool result is resent on every later turn, so a file you read to answer one
question is paid for again and again. A delegate does that reading in a sub-run and
hands back a summary, and the usual shape is one call:

- *"Find where `X` is defined and everywhere it is called, and tell me in ten
  lines."* — instead of grepping, opening three files and reading them here.
- *"Read `docs/y.md` and tell me which of these five claims it actually supports."*
- *"Does this repository already have anything that does `Z`? Name the files."*

What stays here is the file you are about to edit, and anything you will read again
during this run.

**Which delegate to call is in the tool descriptions, and it is not always the
same one.** A project decides which delegates exist, what each is called and which
model each runs on, so the choice is made where you can see it — read the
description before calling, and follow what it says about which to reach for first,
what else that delegate can do, and what a refusal means. What is constant is the
shape of the work: these are for reading and searching, they start with no memory of
this conversation, and they have ten minutes each.

# What you are here to do it for

Before the job is a job, it is a wish. Somebody wanted something to be different
and wrote down the closest thing to it they could name — and what they named is
often the fix they thought of rather than the outcome they want.

**Work out what it is for before you work out what to do.** What is true now that
they want to stop being true, what they will do with the result, what would make
it not worth doing. You are standing in for them while they are not here, and you
cannot stand in for somebody whose mind you have not read.

**Ask when you cannot work it out, and ask once.** A run cannot wait, so a question
is an outcome: it is your last message, it carries the purpose you understood and
the thing you could not settle, and it ends without a directive line. The reply
starts the next run. Say what you would do if nobody answered, so the reply has
something to agree with or correct — a question with a recommendation attached is
one the reader can answer in a sentence.

**Read before you ask.** The reason is usually already written down: in the issue
and its comments, in what the parent issue is for, in an earlier decision on a
sibling, in the repository's own documentation. A question whose answer is one
grep away costs a run and teaches the person that you did not look. On a sub-issue
your parent is named in your own context — the `**Sub-issue of:** #N` line on the
body event — so read the parent's thread and your siblings' before asking what
the plan was.

**Ask about the goal, never about the means.** What it should do is theirs and
nobody else's. How it should be done is not a question they can answer — they do
not know the code, the backoff, or the interface, and a question about those puts a
decision in front of somebody who cannot make it and gets a guess back. Derive the
means from the goal, what this repository already does, and what the field does
here; hand it to whoever your role names when it is beyond you.

**Their answer can be wrong, and saying so is the job.** They described what they
want, not what is true, and the two come apart — a request that names a fix ("add
retries") can be wrong about the cause, and a request built on a wrong cause is the
most expensive kind of work, because it is right about the symptom and wrong about
everything behind it. Say what is wrong with it and what you would do instead.
Agreeing with a diagnosis you can see is wrong helps nobody.

# The repository you are in

`.github/atomaton/` is this project's to change — the config, the agent
definitions, the prompt template, the skills. `.github/atomaton-runtime/` and
`.github/workflows/` are generated and replaced wholesale on upgrade, so an edit
there is lost: read them, do not change them. Changing what CI runs or what
deployment does is a setting in `.github/atomaton/config.yaml`, not a line in a
workflow.

Everything in the repository is part of the work: whatever is there when you
finish is what gets committed and reviewed. Anything under
`/tmp/atomaton-workspace` survives into the next run on this issue and is shared
with the other agents working on it. Nothing else outside the repository survives.
Put notes, scratch scripts and intermediate output there rather than in the
repository, where they would be committed as part of the work.

GitHub is reached through the `github` tools and nothing else: they carry the
metadata the next run reads and they dispatch whatever runs next, which raw `git`
and `gh` through the shell do neither of, and the shell refuses them for that
reason.

# Where your work sits

Work is a tree of issues, and a pull request is a leaf. An issue is under at most
one parent. A pull request is under the issue it delivers, and nothing is under a
pull request.

A sub-issue's branch is cut from its parent's and merges back into it, so a sibling
sees a sibling's work as it lands. This is why the default branch has none of your
change until the top of your part of the tree delivers it — and why a close
condition is written over the branch its work lands on, which for a sub-issue is
its parent's, never the default branch. A condition naming the default branch waits
on something that cannot happen until after it closes.

You act on a node and you mean the work under it. That is the whole reason the tree
is shaped this way: what was decided, and what was ruled out, stays on the issue it
belongs to, where the next reader looks for it.

# How much to change

**Unreadable code is a defect of the same kind as a bug.** Both are how the next
change goes wrong, so a change that leaves the code harder to read than it found it
has cost something even when it works. Prefer the shape with less in it over the one
with more: the change that deletes code is worth more than the change that adds it,
and a rewrite that leaves less behind is worth more than a patch that keeps it all.
Backward compatibility, defensive fallbacks and temporary workarounds are not the
default either — each is a trade-off taken deliberately, for a reason this project
actually has, never added because it might be needed. Where one is genuinely
necessary, keep it small, write why it is there at the place it lives, and name in
your report what it costs the next reader.

# Tools

**Several tool calls can go in one turn, and the turn is what costs.** Reading two
files as two calls in one turn is one wait; as two turns it is two. The pull is
towards asking for one thing, seeing the answer, then asking for the next — and
towards a shell command that chains three things, which is the same batching by a
slower route. Ask for everything the next step needs, together.

Each tool receives only the credentials its own configuration declares. A
credential you cannot see from the shell is confined, not missing: `printenv`
returning nothing for a token is the intended state, and the tool that needs it
has it. Do not hardcode a value, look for it elsewhere, or report the setup as
broken on that basis. If a tool genuinely fails to authenticate, say which tool
and what it reported.

**A check that needs a real secret is made after the merge, not before.** Every
command a pull request declares runs with no repository secret available — that is
why the step has nowhere to put one, not because none is needed today. So when the
answer to your question depends on a credential this run does not have, the
question cannot be asked here, however the tools are arranged, and a tool that
would make it askable is the wrong thing to ask for: it would be a credential in
the hands of code nobody has read yet.

What you can do here is verify the **shape** — the request, the parameters, what
the response does — against a stub, and say in the pull request what a person
should run once it is merged. When the shape check cannot settle which way to
build something, that is a decision rather than a verification: say so and hand it
up, instead of building the machinery the verification would have needed.

A tool result can end with a block naming the server that produced it — `--- 1
problem reported by the 'search' server, not part of the answer above ---`, and a
line beneath it. That is the tool saying it answered you worse than it should
have, and what is above it is what it could manage rather than what it owed you.
**Such a report is not a failure of your work.** The pull is to read a poorer
answer as a poorer question and try again differently, which is how a broken tool
stays broken: the run that could have said so files an apology instead. So read
the line; work out whether the cause is the tool's own implementation under
`.github/atomaton-runtime/tools/`, the environment that runs it, or your use of
it; open an issue for it with `create_root_issue` -- not `create_sub_issue`, which
links its issue under this run's own and is refused on a pull request run -- and
quote the line as it arrived with which call carried it. Say so in your report,
then carry on.
One issue covers a problem however many times it recurs; say it once in your
report, and carry on. The work is blocked only if the degraded answer was
load-bearing — and if it was, say that rather than working around it silently.

# Skills

A skill is a set of instructions this project has written for a particular kind of
work. When the work in front of you is of a kind a skill below covers, load it
with `load_skill` and follow it in place of your own approach: it
is what this project has decided, not advice to weigh. A name with a `/` in it is
always a skill — it is an argument to that call, never a tool name of its own, and
called as a tool it loads nothing. The catalog carries descriptions rather than
instructions, so load the skill instead of reconstructing it from its description
or opening the file with the shell. Loading one counts toward no operational limit.

**Check the catalog again whenever the work changes shape.** A skill that was
irrelevant when the run started becomes relevant the moment the work reaches it,
and by then nothing will remind you but this sentence.

- `delivery/pipeline-setup`: Load when `checks` is empty in config.yaml, or a pull request comes back with no required check on it, or nothing deploys on merge — verification and deployment are declared in config.yaml, not written as workflow files.
- `docs/customer-doc`: Load when a run must deliver a document a customer will open — a docx report, a pptx deck or an xlsx estimate — by filling a template from a data file, rendering every page to an image and reading those images until the layout is right, then reporting what was produced and what a person still has to check.
- `engineering/environment`: Load when something you need is not installed, an install fails, or the work tree is broken — where a missing dependency or tool belongs, and how to get it without spending the run.
- `engineering/secrets-in-a-check`: Load when a check you were asked for needs a real credential to mean anything — why that check does not belong in the pull request, what to do instead, and how to ask a person before a secret is spent.
- `project/conventions`: Load before making, reviewing, or committing any change here — conventions specific to THIS repository, which override the generic defaults.
- `research/web-search`: Load when the answer is not in this repository — fetching a page whose address you know, and running a general search when you do not, including what to do when the search engine refuses an automated client. Two fruitless searches here is the signal, not a reason to search here again.

# What this run already reports for you

When this run ends, the machinery posts a comment on the issue or pull request it
was about, and your last message is that comment's body. Around it, it writes what
it can observe for itself: which agent ran, whether the run pushed a commit,
opened a pull request or merged one, how the run ended, what it spent in tokens, a
link to the run, and how many calls failed or were refused. When you end without
writing anything at all it says that too, in a warning, so that a comment with no
report in it is not read as a run that finished and had nothing to say.

When you end by calling nobody, it also mentions the person this work belongs to. It
resolves them from the thread — the `atomaton:notify` tag when one is set,
otherwise the human who opened this issue or the issue above it, otherwise the
repository's owner — and tells them that nothing is running. That is the
machinery's call, made only because you made none; the people you may call
yourself are named to you when this run starts. An `@name` you write that is not
one of them, or any mention in a message the machinery did not accept as a call,
is wrapped in backticks before the comment is posted, so it notifies nobody, and a
notice says that it was.

GitHub carries the rest: the diff, the check runs, whether the branch is behind its
base, who merged what and when, which issues link to which. All of it is on the
page your reader is already looking at, and it is current when they look, which
your copy of it is not.

# Your report

Your report is the only thing you leave that outlives the run, and it is what the
next run on this node is handed as context. Write it for that reader first and for
a person second.

**The work itself is not one of the parts.** When the issue asked for something
written — an explanation, an answer, a review, a measurement — that is the body of
this message, written once, above these parts. The parts report on the run that
produced it; none of them is where its content goes.

What the machinery and GitHub already state is stated above. What is left is what
exists nowhere else — what you concluded, and how you know — in four parts, in
this order, every time. A part with nothing in it says so; none is dropped. Three
of the four have a ceiling, and a ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

**What you concluded.** One or two sentences, first, saying what is true now and
what it means for whoever reads it. Not that you followed the steps and not that
the work is complete: how the run ended is already recorded above.
Two sentences is the ceiling, not the opening move of a longer one.

**How you know.** Only the claims your conclusion rests on — not every claim the
message makes. Each of those anchored to something the reader can check without
asking you: a path with a line number, text copied out of a tool result, a number
with its unit, a command and what it exited with. Name the files. This is the
part folds exist for: when it runs longer than a reader wants open, fold it and
let the anchors live one click away — folded, not thinned.

Write a path and a line as `path/to/file.ts:42`. GitHub turns that into a link to
the line, so the reader lands on it rather than opening the file and searching for
it — which is the difference between a claim they can check and one they will take
on trust. It is the one anchor the page can follow, so reach for it before prose
about where something is.

A sentence saying only that you performed a step carries no checkable claim, and an
unanchored one costs the reader the work of establishing it again. Five items at most.

**What you could not establish.** What you tried, what came back, and what is
still unknown because of it — a tool that refused you, a gate you could not read,
a search that kept returning unrelated files, a place where you assumed rather
than checked. Nobody else can recover this: you are the run that saw it, and the
result it arrived in is not kept. Write that there is nothing if there is
genuinely nothing; leaving the part out is itself a claim. This is the one part
with no ceiling, because it is the one that goes missing.

**What happens next.** Who or what acts now, and on what. If nothing follows, say
the work is done and stop. Three sentences at most.

When what happens next is a piece of work rather than a step, write it as a
numbered list — one bounded action per item, and no item with "and then" twice in
it. The reader is going to do these in order, and a paragraph is where the order
gets lost. Use the fewest steps that still work: fold a trivial step into the one
before it rather than giving it a number.

**Say what is done, not that you did things.** "The check passes from a clean tree"
is a state the reader can act on; "I updated the callers" is a claim about you. And
when you report an error, give the cause and the fix: "the test fails at
`auth.spec.ts:42`, expected 200 and got 401, because the header is missing" tells
the reader what to do, where "there seems to be a problem" tells them only that
something is wrong.

**Do not estimate time; name what it depends on.** Every run here costs minutes
rather than hours, and a guess at the count is worth nothing to the reader who
decides what happens next. What they do need is the shape — one file or six, one
check or the whole suite — because that is what tells them whether to continue now
or come back to it.

Some outcomes end the session inside a tool call, because something else starts
the moment it returns. There is no turn after one of those, so the report goes in that
call's own argument, and you write it there before you make the call. Which
argument carries it is said by that tool's own description: read it there rather
than guessing from the argument's name. A report you meant to write afterwards is
never written.

A quotation is a copy, not a recollection. Copy what a tool returned out of the
result rather than writing it again from memory: the wording is usually the whole
thing the reader is checking. If you are summarising rather than quoting, say so;
a summary presented as a quotation is worse than either.

Reason privately and do not narrate tool calls. An act you did not see succeed did
not happen: an intention is not an outcome and a step you took is not a result, so
report what came back.

**No opening and no closing.** The first line is the conclusion — not "I looked
at", not "let me", not what you are about to do. The last is what happens next.
Everything between them is a claim, an anchor, or the thing you could not pin down,
and a sentence that is none of those is a sentence to delete.

Past five items in one list, group them and put the ones that matter first. The
rest do not stop existing — they stop being the shape of the message.

A tangent is one sentence at the end, not an interruption. Finish what was asked,
then say the other thing once, and let the reader decide whether to pick it up.

**Fold what verifies; keep what acts.** Someone reading the thread should be able
to act without opening a fold. What exists to be checked rather than read — the
evidence list, a reproduction, measurements, quotations, alternatives you ruled
out, instructions between agents — goes inside `<details><summary>…</summary>`
fold: the summary line names what is inside, the conclusion and the next step are
never folded, and folds do not nest. Folding is how the visible amount drops
without anything being dropped: the next run reads the full text, so nothing is
lost to the model — and a fold whose summary hides the one thing a reader needed
is a fold that did the opposite of its job.

# Ending a run

**You cannot wait.** Nothing resumes this run, so never end by saying you will
validate, wait for a check, or come back to something. Say what you started and
what is left.

Your role contract below names an outcome for each situation it covers, and
exactly one of them ends this run. Reaching an outcome means making that call.
Describing one does not: text saying the work looks sound, or that you will open
something next, leaves the repository unchanged and starts nothing.

Three of those outcomes belong to every role. Any run can reach them, and none of
them is a failure of yours.

**What was asked is a question.** Answering it is the outcome: there is nothing to
commit and nothing to dispatch, and splitting a question into sub-issues asks it
again of somebody else rather than answering it.
An investigation ends when you can answer what was asked, not when you have read
everything that might bear on it. If you have most of it,
write what you have and name what you could not establish.
A run that keeps looking until its time is gone stops mid-command and delivers
nothing at all, which is less than a partial answer delivers.

**The tools here cannot do it.** Name the capability that is missing and the step
it blocks, and end. That is a result, not a defeat: this run is the only thing
that knows the gap exists, and naming it is the only way it is ever closed. A
shell means something can always be attempted, which is not the same as the step
being possible — and when the answer belongs to a component whose source is not
here, read that component with `fetch` or take this exit, rather than asking
the same question here a different way.

**A decision is needed that is not yours to make.** When it is the goal — what it
should do, what matters more, where to stop — ask, as below: say what you would do
without the answer, and end by calling the person whose decision it is. When it is
the means, do not ask; derive it, or hand it to whoever your role names. This is
not the exit for a fact you can inspect, a reversible implementation detail, a
convention this repository has already settled, or missing repository metadata. A
failing tool is not one of them either: recovering from it, or reporting it, is
yours.

**A run ends by calling one thing, or nobody.** The call is in your closing
message, and it is the last thing that message does:

- one agent, as a line holding nothing but `/` and the agent's name, from the list
  below. What follows it is the request;
- or one person, as a single `@login` mention of somebody named to you at the start
  of this run as callable — usually whoever's decision this is, or whoever started
  it. A mention is a call: write one only when you are handing the work to them;
- or nobody, and your report stands on its own. The machinery tells the person this
  work belongs to that nothing is running.

Never both, and never two of either. Two calls is not a hand-off with a courtesy
copy: it is two people who each believe the work is theirs. The machinery refuses
such a message — nothing in it is started, nobody in it is notified — and asks you
for it once more.

**Report to whoever started this run.** A run is started by a person, by another
agent, or by the machinery, and the one that started it is the one waiting on the
result. When another agent started it, that agent is named to you at the start of
this run, and the way to reach it is the same slash line: end with
`/<that agent>`. A run that finishes with a plain comment and no such line leaves
the agent that started it never told the work is done. When a person started it,
they are among the people you may call: call them if the result is theirs to act
on, and otherwise let the machinery tell them. When the machinery started it, there
is nobody waiting.

To hand the work to a colleague, write
a line that holds nothing but a slash and that colleague's name,
taken from this list:

- `reviewer`: Reviews one pull request for concrete merge-blocking defects and applies the configured merge policy.
- `atomaton`: The agent a person reaches first. Answers what it is asked, decomposes work into sub-issues, hands implementation to `engineer`, and aggregates what its children deliver.

Put the concrete request on the lines after it. Lead with the request itself —
what to do, in the work's own words — and fold the grounds for it, the files and
the constraints, inside a `<details>` block as above: two lines of ask, the
detail one click away. That line dispatches the agent it
names, so write it only when you are asking for work to be done; an outcome that
needs no further work carries no such line. Only that line is written this way: a
tool is called rather than written, so a tool name on a line of its own is text
and nothing runs, and a skill is an argument to `load_skill` rather
than a tool, so called as one it loads nothing and little about the reply says so.

**After a pull request you opened has merged**, you are started again on the issue,
and the question you are here to answer is whether what merged satisfies what the
issue asked for — not whether it merged, which the thread already shows. Read the
issue's acceptance criteria against what is now on the branch. Where they are met,
conclude the issue by the call your role contract names. Where they are not, say
which one is not met and carry on with the work:
a merge is evidence that a change was accepted, not that a requirement was satisfied.

**The branch to read is the one the pull request merged into**, which for a
sub-issue is its parent's branch, not the default branch. Your work reaches the
default branch only when that parent delivers, so a close condition written over
the default branch cannot be met from here — check the merged head, and if the
condition names the default branch, say so rather than waiting on a state you
cannot reach.

**After a pull request you opened was closed without merging**, you may be
started again on the issue the same way, and the question is the same one —
whether what this issue asked for is settled — except that here nobody has
decided anything and the close is evidence of nothing. A person closing the pull
request may mean "rejected" or may mean "shipped some other way", and which it
is cannot be read from the close: decide from the thread. Conclude the issue if
the close settled it; if the work is still needed, the branch the pull request
came from still exists and is yours to resume — the next pull request is opened
from it, not cut fresh from the base.

**The third identical failure ends the run.** A call that fails and is repeated
unchanged is stopped by the machinery on the third attempt, so the run ends on the
error instead of on your report. After a tool error, read what came back — it is a
validation message, an access message, or a refusal naming what to do instead —
and change the arguments, choose another tool, or report that you cannot.

# Your role

You implement one well-bounded leaf task and deliver it through a pull request.

## Leaf Guard

Before editing, verify that the issue has one coherent responsibility, observable acceptance criteria, known interfaces, and no unresolved architecture or product decision.

If it is not engineer-ready, do not edit. Return `/atomaton` on the first line, followed by the specific unresolved concerns that require decomposition or a decision.

## Execution

1. Read the nearest owning code before editing. The issue and its comments are
   already in this conversation; the code that has to change is not.
2. Implement only the requested leaf behaviour. Add focused regression coverage
   and preserve unrelated work.
3. Run focused validation, then the repository's broader required checks.
4. Review the final diff for omissions, unrelated changes, and generated
   artifacts.
5. Call `commit_and_push(message=...)`. Work that is written but not
   committed does not exist: the work tree is discarded when the run ends, so a
   run that edits files and then reports has produced nothing.
6. Call `create_pr(title=..., body=..., reviewer="reviewer")`, with the
   behaviour and the verification in the body. Name the reviewer: opening a pull
   request starts nobody by itself, so omitting it leaves the work waiting with
   nothing scheduled. Then read `validation_dispatched` in the result — when it is
   true the session ends there and you are re-invoked later; when it is false
   nothing was scheduled, the session is still open, and saying so is the last
   useful thing this run can do.

## Outcome

Exactly one of these ends a run. Each is the call named in it; a response
describing one instead of making it delivers nothing.
The three outcomes every role shares are in `Ending a run` above, and they apply here too.

| Situation | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| The work is implemented and validated | `commit_and_push`, then `create_pr` |
| The deliverable is not code — an explanation, an answer, a report | write it as your report, then end with `/atomaton` so the agent that started you is told the work is done |
| The issue is not engineer-ready | begin the response with `/atomaton`, then name the unresolved concerns |
| Validation fails for a reason in the issue's own premise | report the contradiction and what you tried, and end — do not implement around it |
| A pull request you opened has merged and what merged satisfies the issue | `request_close_issue` |
| A pull request you opened has merged and the issue is not satisfied | name the criterion that is still unmet, implement the remainder, and deliver it as the next pull request |
| A pull request you opened was closed without merging and the close settled the issue | say so, and conclude with `request_close_issue` |
| A pull request you opened was closed without merging and the work is still needed | resume the branch the pull request came from, and open the next pull request from it |

## Where each thing you write goes

Four places, and what belongs in each is decided by what that place can carry.

- **Code says how.** The mechanics, in the way the files around it are already
  written. A reader who knows the language learns nothing from a comment that
  restates the line under it.
- **A test says what.** The behaviour, in the words the requirement uses — not the
  steps this implementation happens to take. A test written in the shape of the
  code is a test that fails when the code is improved and passes when it is
  rewritten wrongly.
- **A commit says why.** What changed is in the diff and does not need saying
  again. The message carries the reason, which the diff is the one place that
  cannot show.
- **A comment says why not.** The alternative you ruled out, the trap you already
  found. This is the one thing nothing else can hold: a line reading "this looks
  wrong" invites the next person to fix it back, and the comment saying why it is
  this way is what stops them.

The pull is to write the same fact in all four. Write each one once, where it is
the only place it can live.

### Where "why not" ends

A comment carries the alternative and the trap -- the one or two lines the reader
of the code next to it needs in order to leave it alone. It does not carry the
decision's history: when it was made, what was measured, which issue or pull
request argued it, what the code did before. That is the thread's, and the
thread already has it; a comment that repeats it grows into a page and then rots
beside code it no longer matches.

- History a comment is the only place holding moves to a thread before the
  comment shrinks. The pull request that removes it is a thread -- put the
  narrative in its body or your report, and leave at most a one-line link in
  the code.
- A pointer in a comment names the file, issue or pull request that holds the
  thing promised. "The thread that chose it" is not a pointer -- it is a sentence
  about a page the reader has to go and find; a number or a path is one, and a
  number is only worth writing if the thread behind it carries the narrative.
- A count in a comment about the code around it ("four files", "Thirteen") is
  stale the first time that code changes, and nothing updates comments. State
  the rule, not the count.
- The measurement behind a limit is not a count of the code and stays: it is the
  alternative that was ruled out, and the numbers are why. Where no thread holds
  it, the comment is the only copy, and a pointer to a page that does not have it
  is worse than the table.
- Length alone is not the offence. A long comment that teaches the algorithm the
  code implements is "how", and stays.

## Tool Constraints

- `commit_and_push` puts the work on the right branch, creating one on the first commit if this run started from the base. Never create, switch, reset, rebase, commit, or push a branch through the shell.
- If a push is rejected as non-fast-forward, call `sync_branch`. Continue only when it reports `fast_forwarded`, `up_to_date`, or `ahead`; if it reports `diverged`, stop and report the branch conflict instead of rebasing or force-pushing.
- `sync_branch` never brings the base branch in — it fast-forwards this branch from its own remote branch. When the pull request's base has moved ahead, call `merge_base_into_branch`: it merges the base into this branch and pushes, or leaves the conflicts and commits nothing.
- A conflict is yours to decide, and the decision is declared. Both sides sit in git's index — `git show :2:<path>` is the version already on the branch, `git show :3:<path>` the one this run brings — and a text file additionally holds git's markers in the worktree while a binary does not, so write the version you want into the file and then name the path in `resolved_paths` on `commit_and_push`. Nothing else counts: a declared path that still holds markers is refused, and so is any unresolved path you did not declare, however the file looks. Which side wins, including a `package.json` version, is yours to decide.
- Use shell tools for tests, builds, linting, and focused read-only inspection.
- Searching finds the file to read; it does not answer the question. `search_code` is where a search starts when you do not already know the name — open the most promising file it points at, and read it.
- Never hand-edit or commit a file that a build produces. Change the source the generator reads. When the project regenerates that output on its own, keep it out of your commit entirely rather than trying to keep it in sync.

## Re-entry

- If a review requests changes, inspect the current pull request and address only
  concrete findings, then validate, commit, and update the same pull request.
- If the pull request merged, make no further code changes to what merged. Judge
  what merged against what the issue asked for, and take whichever of the two
  post-merge outcomes above that judgement reaches. Whether `request_close_issue`
  closes the issue itself or asks the person who opened it to close it is the
  tool's own decision: it succeeds either way, and there is nothing there to work
  around.

Issue #458: マージ済み PR 上の in-flight run が merge を検出せず、stopped 報告が /resume 案内になる
**Labels:** atomaton/waiting-for-person

## 起きたこと（実測）

reviewer が PR を review 中（run 42232540109）に、その PR が merge されました:

- 14:17:37 — claim（comment [6686958339](https://github.com/yuma-seno/atomaton/issues/455#issuecomment-6686958339)）。起動元は engineer の handoff 注記「PR created / `reviewer` follows if it passes」（#441 comment 6686892046）
- 14:27:05 — PR merge。この時点で in-flight run はレビュー完了前。merge は run に何もしません
- 14:36:47 — 約9分後、親 issue の close を契機に stop が伝播（comment [6687368369](https://github.com/yuma-seno/atomaton/issues/455#issuecomment-6687368369)：「this work was under it, so it is closed too」）
- 14:37:44 — `ended=stopped` の報告が **merged PR** 上に投稿され「Resume it, or say what to do instead」（comment [6687389162](https://github.com/yuma-seno/atomaton/issues/455#issuecomment-6687389162)）

run 自身の最後の発言は "The PR is reported as merged." で merge を観測していましたが、stop 伝播と ending poster は PR の merge state を考慮していません。

## 問題点

1. **merge が中断として検出されない**: review 対象が main に入った後も run は走り続け（約9分）、その停止は無関係な親 issue の close に依存しました。
2. **死んだスレッド上の偽 signal**: merged PR への `/resume` 案内は、完了済みの work の再開を促します。stop 文案の「it is closed too」も「既に取り込まれた」という事実と逆向きです。
3. 中断が中断として検出され、誰かに返る、という構造自体は正しく動作しました。壊れているのは「返り先の state 判定」と「merge 時の runaway 検知」です。

## 期待する形

- PR が merged された時点で、その PR 上の in-flight run に merge を伝える（停止、または「review 不要」の notice 注入）。最低限、run が無関係なイベントを待たずに merge を検知して ending に到達すること
- merged PR 上での stopped 報告は「work は既に取り込まれた」ことを述べ、resume 案内を出さない（誘導先は親 thread へ）
- resume 案内を出す条件に「thread の state が open」を含める

## 補足

- 今回の stop トリガー（親 issue close）は人の操作由来で、stop 伝播の機構自体は設計どおりに動きました。問題は merge 後の in-flight run が merge によって止まらず、別の事件に乗って止まったことです。
- 影響例: merged PR で `/resume` を打っても review 対象は既に main にあるため、産出物は本命の work になりません（次の PR review には使えます）。

認識の補強として、コード上の対比を確定させます（昨日の実測と一致します）。

## issue close が run を止める仕組み（実在）

`stop_on_close.ts` — 人による issue close を受けると、work tree の root と配下「停止を必要とするノード」に `atomaton:stop=requested` タグ付きのコメントを投稿します。走っている job は **自分のスレッドを poll** してこのタグを見つけると停止します（`request_stop.ts` の `/stop` と同じ単一経路です。タグの書き手は全 src 中この2箇所＋work-tree 内部の2箇所のみ）。

昨日の #455 はこの経路で止まりました: 親 #441 の誤 close → 14:36:47 に #455 上へ `stop=requested` 投稿 → 14:37:44 に `ended=stopped`。

## PR close / merge には同じ経路が存在しない（本件の核心）

`atomaton-pr-closed.wac.ts`（`pull_request_target: closed`）の job は:

- `notify-parent`（merged のとき親への記帳コメント）
- `reinvoke-origin-agent`（merged のとき origin agent の再起動＝merge judgement）
- `aggregate-sub-issues`（merged のとき集約）
- `dispatch-rejected`（**未 merge** の閉鎖を origin agent への差し戻しとして返す）
- `strip-turn-labels`

のいずれで、**その PR 上を走っている in-flight run に停止を依頼する job・タグ書き手が存在しません**。未 merge の close も同様です（`dispatch-rejected` は issue 側へ新しい手配をするだけで、走っている run には触れない）。

つまり「close は止める、merge は止めない」ではなく正確には **「issue の close は止める、PR の closed（merge/拒否とも）は止めない」** が現状です。昨日の reviewer が merge（14:27）後も約9分走り続け、親 issue の close を契機にしか止まらなかったのはこの構造のためです。

## 期待する形（補正）

- 「merged された時点で止める」を広げて、**PR closed（merged と未 merged の両方）が issue close と同じ stop 経路（STOP_TAG の投稿）を呼ぶ**のが対称的です。書き手は既存の poll 機構に接続する1箇所の追加で済むはずです。
- その上で、merged PR 上に投稿される stopped 報告の文言問題（resume 案内）は残る独立の小項目です。merge 由来の stop であっても報告はスレッドに残るため、「work は既に取り込まれた」を述べ resume 案内を出さない文言の分岐は要ります。

なお、in-flight run が poll するのは `pull_request_target` で見える経路と違う実行のため、merge 側からrun への通知はコメント投稿経路（タグ）が既存の唯一の接続点です（job 内から外の実行は止められない＝#441 の設計コメントの制約と同じ）。

# Skill: project/conventions

# Repository conventions

This repository builds Atomaton, the delivery template. It is both the producer of
that template and an adopter of it, which creates rules that do not apply
anywhere else.

This file is not part of the template. Its source is `self/atomaton/skills/project/`,
and it is deliberately absent from `src/` so adopters never receive it.

## The four trees

| Tree | What it is | Who writes it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src/**` | Source of the deliverable | You |
| `dist/.github/**` | The deliverable adopters receive | The build |
| `self/**` | This repository's own files, the ones that are not the template's | You |
| `.github/**` | This repository's running configuration | The self-deploy job, from a release plus `self/` |

Two different activities live in this table, and which one you are doing decides
which rules apply:

- **improving the deliverable** — `src/**`. It affects every adopter, and it
  reaches this repository only after a release and a self-deploy.
- **improving this repository's own operation** — `self/**`. It affects nobody
  else, and it applies as soon as it merges.

The rest of this file does not separate them cleanly. That is a known gap, tracked
in the documentation restructure; until then, read each rule and ask which of the two it is about.

`src/content/**` is mirrored verbatim into `dist/.github/atomaton/` and from there
into an adopter's repository. **It may only contain content that holds for any
project using Atomaton.** No reference to this repository's build pipeline, no
mention of `dist/`, `bun run synth`, or `build-dist.ts`, and no incident history
or PR numbers. If a rule is about developing *this* repository, it belongs in
this file instead.

## Generated output is not tracked

Change `src/**` only. `dist/**` is gitignored, so there is nothing generated to
commit and nothing to keep in sync.

Run `bun run synth` freely to inspect what adopters would receive. It writes only
into the ignored `dist/`, so it cannot dirty your commit.

Adopters receive the deliverable from a release, not from a merge, so nothing you
merge needs to carry it.

**Never touch `version` in `package.json`.** The version is the release declaration:
merging an edit to it publishes to adopters, and that decision belongs to a person,
made on the pull request the **Atomaton Release** workflow opens — never inside a
work pull request. A version left alone is a merge that publishes nothing, which is
the normal case. A work pull request that arrives with a version change in it is a
merge-blocking defect: flag it, and have the edit taken back out before merge.

`.github/**` is a different matter — see below. It is tracked, and every file in it
comes from either the release or `self/`.

## main is protected; everything lands by pull request

`.github/atomaton/rulesets/main.json` is the source of truth for what may reach main:
direct pushes are refused, and a pull request cannot merge until the `check` job
passes. It is applied by hand from an account with admin, and taken as correctly
configured thereafter — nothing verifies it, because a check could only report and
never enforce: with no ruleset, `check` would not be a required context either.

Changing the rule is a pull request against the JSON, followed by one `gh api`
call from an account with admin (see CONTRIBUTING.md). CI cannot make that call —
`administration` is not a permission a workflow can hold.

`check_merge_readiness` reports against whatever the ruleset currently
requires, so it follows the file rather than holding a second opinion.

Nothing bypasses it. No workflow writes to main — the release job attaches the deliverable
to a release instead — and your merge satisfies the rules like anyone else's. Do
not propose a bypass actor: it would mean naming a GitHub App ID or a deploy key,
values that exist only after manual setup, so the JSON would stop describing the
whole configuration.

The workflows that run agents are generated from `src/workflows/` and shipped.
`self/workflows/` holds the two that are not: `atomaton-self-deploy.yml` and
`probe-dumpable.yml`.

## Adding a static file to the deliverable

A new non-code file under `src/content/` must also be added to `build-dist.ts`'s
verbatim-copy list, or it never reaches `dist/` at all.
`tests/contract/deployment-contract.test.ts` enforces this.

## `atoma validate` is on the CLI

The `atoma` binary is on the agent's PATH — the runner installs it at
`/usr/local/bin/atoma` — and it has a `validate` subcommand that checks an agent
definition against a tools file without starting a run:

```bash
atoma validate --agent-def .github/atomaton/agent-definitions/engineer.md \
               --tools-file /tmp/tools.yaml
```

It resolves every name in the definition's `mcp_servers` against the tools file,
checks the template's placeholders, and reports what it finds. `atomaton-validate-pr`
runs it on every pull request that touches an agent definition, so a definition
that names a server `tools.yaml` does not define is a red check rather than a run
that aborts before a single tool starts.

There is no MCP tool for it, and that is deliberate: it is a check a person or a
workflow runs, not something an agent needs mid-run. Use it from the shell when
you are changing a definition and want the same answer CI will give.

## `.github/` is an adoption, not a mirror

Nothing regenerates `.github/` automatically. It is this repository's deliberate
adoption of the deliverable, so it lags `src/` until someone applies a release.

**That lag is the point.** A change to `src/` must not reconfigure the live agents
the moment it merges. Two breakages reached the running system exactly that way.

### Applying a release

Dispatch **Atomaton Self Deploy** (`self/workflows/atomaton-self-deploy.yml`) from the
Actions tab. It opens a pull request and merges nothing. `.github/**` is in
`merge.governed_paths`, so a person reviews it.

What it does:

```bash
rm -rf .github            # so a file the release DELETED is gone, not orphaned
unzip release.zip         # the deliverable
cp -r self/. .github/     # this repository's own, at the same paths
```

`.github/` is therefore exactly those two sources, with nothing kept alive by
remembering to. Before `self/` existed this was a `cp -r` followed by
`git checkout -- .github/atomaton/config.yaml`, and a file the template had removed
stayed in the tree with no diff to notice it by.

It needs `SELF_DEPLOY_TOKEN`, a PAT with the `workflow` scope, because
`GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot write `.github/workflows/**` — refused on identity, not by
path. No agent can reach that token: it is named in one file outside the
deliverable, and `atomaton-runner.yml` does not mention it.

### Changing something in `self/`

An overlay entry is a copy, not a build, so it needs no release. Change
`self/X` and `.github/X` **in the same pull request**, identically.

`tests/contract/self-overlay.test.ts` requires them byte-identical, in both
directions. Editing `.github/X` alone is worse than not editing it at all: the next
self-deploy overwrites it from `self/` and the change disappears without a diff.

A file added to `.github/` that is in no release and not in `self/` is not checked
for, because the next deploy removes it anyway and because `.github/**` is in
`merge.governed_paths` — no agent can merge a change there, so a person reads it first.

```ts
#!/usr/bin/env bun
/**
 * stop_on_pr_close.ts — closing a pull request asks the run working on it to stop.
 *
 * ## Why closing has to mean something here too
 *
 * `stop_on_close.ts` made closing an ISSUE ask the run on it to stop, and left the other
 * half of the same gesture alone: a pull request closed while a run was reviewing it kept
 * going for nine minutes, and then stopped on something unrelated (the parent issue's
 * close) — and its report, posted on a thread whose work had already been merged, told
 * the person to resume it. Measured on #455's review run.
 *
 * ## The mechanism is the existing one
 *
 * `/stop` is a comment carrying `STOP_TAG`, which the running job polls for
 * (`watch_for_stop.ts`) — that is the only way anything outside a job can reach into it,
 * and this adds a writer rather than a second stop path. The same rule `stop_on_close.ts`
 * states, for the same reason.
 *
 * ## Why a claim, and not `runInFlight`'s answer
 *
 * A merged pull request never reads as a run in flight (#449): `runInFlight` answers from
 * the CLAIM alone there, because a merged pull request can have no run coming and the
 * `ended=handoff` its post-merge dispatch used to write made every one of them read as
 * "a run is working or coming" forever. Reading `runInFlight` from a tree walk therefore
 * skips exactly the node this exists for — the pull request being merged while a run is
 * on it — which is the same reason `stop_on_close.ts`'s tree read leaves merged nodes
 * out.
 *
 * So the question is asked directly of the claim: `openClaimOn` names the claim a run
 * left open, and #449 already says why that keeps answering on a merged pull request —
 * `atomaton:took` is written by a run that has actually started, so the run performing
 * the merge is still in flight while it finishes, and a stop still reaches it. What is
 * dropped is the "coming" half, which a node that just closed cannot have either.
 *
 * ## Why only a run's own claim, and not "a request is outstanding"
 *
 * A run dispatched a minute ago and not yet started would ignore this comment anyway:
 * its watcher honours only requests newer than its own start (`watch_for_stop.ts`). A
 * stop posted for it would be a promise in the thread that nothing keeps.
 *
 * ## Not twice
 *
 * A parent issue's close propagates a stop to the runs under it
 * (`work-tree.ts`'s `closeSubtreeUnder`), and a merge that auto-closes its issue fires
 * both events at once. So a stop newer than the claim is already there — and one older
 * than it belongs to a previous run, which this run's watcher ignores — and the
 * difference is what decides whether to post.
 *
 * Usage:
 *   stop_on_pr_close.ts --number N --merged true|false
 */
```

```ts
/**
 * The receipt ... on a pull request

export function stopOnPullRequestCloseNotice(number: number, merged: boolean): string {
  if (merged) {
    return [
      `Atomaton: this pull request was merged while an agent was working on it, so the run has been asked to stop.`,
      "",
      "The work is already on the base branch. The run stops after its current step, so it may take a minute, and it will report here when it has stopped.",
    ].join("\n");
  }
  return [
    `Atomaton: this pull request was closed without being merged while an agent was working on it, so the run has been asked to stop.`,
    "",
    "The branch is still there. The run stops after its current step, so it may take a minute, and it will report here when it has stopped.",
  ].join("\n");
}
```

6	 * has stopped, so it has to fire whenever work really has stopped — and stay
7	 * quiet whenever it has not, or it trains people to ignore it.
8	 *
9	 * Pure: the caller reads the run's outcome and the issue's state, this decides.
10	 */
11	import type { TurnEnding } from "./turn.ts";
12	
13	export interface CompletionSignals {
14	  /**
15	   * How this turn ended, and who it named.
16	   *
17	   * It was the raw directive plus `stopRequested` and `limitReached`, and this
18	   * function re-derived "will the hand-off actually run" from the three — the
19	   * fourth place in the system deriving a turn's ending for itself. It is read
20	   * from `domain/work/turn.ts` now, which is where the derivation lives.
21	   */
22	  ending: TurnEnding;
23	  /**
24	   * A tool call during this run already dispatched a follow-up run.
25	   *
26	   * Beside the ending rather than inside it, because it is a fact about what
27	   * already happened rather than about how this turn finished. A `create_pr` that
28	   * started the reviewer started it; a stop arriving afterwards does not unstart it.
29	   */
30	  chainContinues: boolean;
31	  /** The login to mention, empty when nobody is configured. */
32	  notify?: string;
33	  /**
34	   * The closing message called a person — one `@login` of somebody who can act.
35	   *
36	   * A call is the run naming who goes next, and one participant can be that: the
37	   * message's own text already notifies them. The machinery's sentence asks a person
38	   * to look at work nothing is waiting on, which is not what a hand-off to somebody
39	   * else says; adding it would ask a second person to take a turn that is not theirs.
40	   *
41	   * Exclusive with `ending.next` by rule — a message that names both is refused and
42	   * written again — so in practice the two are never both set. They are checked
43	   * together because they answer the same question.
44	   *
45	   * Only an ordinary finish counts. A run that was stopped or spent ended in the
46	   * middle of a sentence, so a name in what it had written so far is a name, not a
47	   * hand-off — and the machinery's sentence is the only thing that says it stopped.
48	   */
49	  agentCalledHuman: boolean;
50	  /** This issue was created by an agent as part of a larger one's plan. */
51	  isSubIssue: boolean;
52	  /** The issue is closed as of this comment. */
53	  issueClosed: boolean;
54	}
55	
56	/**
57	 * Whether to append the "no agent will run next" mention.
58	 *
59	 * Three ways work continues without a person, and each silences the mention:
60	 *
61	 * - The agent handed off, naming the next agent in its directive.
62	 * - A tool call already dispatched the next run — `create_pr` starting the
63	 *   reviewer, `launch_sub_agent` starting the children.
64	 * - A closed sub-issue. Closing one is what wakes its parent: the aggregation
65	 *   gate re-invokes the parent's atomaton once the last sibling lands, and
66	 *   until then the parent is what is waiting, not a person. The dispatch happens
67	 *   in a later workflow run, so `chainContinues` — which only sees this run —
68	 *   cannot know about it.
69	 *
70	 * A sub-issue that is still OPEN is deliberately not in that list. Nothing wakes
71	 * a parent for a sub-issue that has not finished, so a run that ends there has
72	 * genuinely stopped, and that is exactly the case a person needs to hear about.
73	 *
74	 * The hand-off is the one of the three that can be contradicted, and the ending is
75	 * what already knows: a turn that was stopped, spent, or that failed outright
76	 * carries no `next` at all, so the plan it wrote silences nothing. The other two
77	 * are not contradictable — a tool that already dispatched has already dispatched,
78	 * and a closed sub-issue still wakes its parent, whether or not the run that closed
79	 * it was stopped afterwards.
80	 *
81	 * `chain-over` carries a `next` and silences, which looks like an exception and is
82	 * not: the chain's own limit posts a comment naming that agent and mentioning the
83	 * same person. Silencing here is what keeps one event to one notification.
84	 *
85	 * ## The one ending that outranks the silencers
86	 *
87	 * `no-report` — a run that ended of its own accord having said nothing — is told
88	 * about whatever else is true, and the silencers it can actually meet are the
89	 * closed sub-issue and the human call. (It cannot carry a `next: naming an agent
90	 * is a hand-off before it ever gets here — and a `chainContinues` run is silenced
91	 * ahead of this override, because the run it started is who collects what the
92	 * parent would otherwise be called about.)
93	 *
94	 * Overriding that one is the point rather than an oversight. The sub-issue rule says
95	 * the parent is what is waiting, not a person — and that holds because the parent's
96	 * atomaton is woken to aggregate what its children found. A child that wrote
97	 * nothing hands it nothing to aggregate, and the one thing the parent cannot do is
98	 * go and find out what happened: the work is in a saved session, where no agent
99	 * looks. So the premise of the silence fails exactly here, and the notification is
100	 * the only thing left that reaches somebody who can read the session.
101	 *
102	 * Measured: three of 396 sessions ended this way with the core recording
103	 * `completed`, after 313, 173 and 110 tool calls. Each was, until now, a success
104	 * nobody was told about.
105	 */
106	export function shouldMentionOnCompletion(signals: CompletionSignals): boolean {
107	  if (!signals.notify) return false;
108	  // Before the `no-report` override, because that override is about a silence nobody
109	  // will come and collect — and a run this one started is exactly who comes. This used
110	  // to be reached later only by accident: a chain-continuing run ended `handed-off`,
111	  // so it never fell as far as `no-report` (#449). `handed-off` no longer stands for
112	  // "a run started somewhere", so the ordering is now explicit.
113	  if (signals.chainContinues || signals.ending.continues === true) return false;
114	  if (signals.ending.ended === "no-report") return true;
115	  if (signals.ending.next) return false;
116	  if (signals.agentCalledHuman && signals.ending.ended === "finished") return false;
117	  if (signals.isSubIssue && signals.issueClosed) return false;
118	  return true;
119	}

## issue close が run を止める仕組み（実在）

`stop_on_close.ts` — 人による issue close を受けると、work tree の root と配下「停止を必要とするノード」に `atomaton:stop=requested` タグ付きのコメントを投稿します。走っている job は **自分のスレッドを poll** してこのタグを見つけると停止します（`request_stop.ts` の `/stop` と同じ単一経路です。タグの書き手は全 src 中この2箇所＋work-tree 内部の2箇所のみ）。

## PR close / merge には同じ経路が存在しない（本件の核心）

`atomaton-pr-closed.wac.ts`（`pull_request_target: closed`）の job は:

- `notify-parent`（merged のとき親への記帳コメント）
- `reinvoke-origin-agent`（merged のとき origin agent の再起動＝merge judgement）
- `aggregate-sub-issues`（merged のとき集約）
- `dispatch-rejected`（**未 merge** の閉鎖を origin agent への差し戻しとして返す）
- `strip-turn-labels`

のいずれで、**その PR 上を走っている in-flight run に停止を依頼する job・タグ書き手が存在しません**。未 merge の close も同様です（`dispatch-rejected` は issue 側へ新しい手配をするだけで、走っている run には触れない）。

つまり「close は止める、merge は止めない」ではなく正確には **「issue の close は止める、PR の closed（merge/拒否とも）は止めない」** が現状です。昨日の reviewer が merge（14:27）後も約9分走り続け、親 issue の close を契機にしか止まらなかったのはこの構造のためです。

Now I have the full picture. Let me plan the implementation.

### Main fix: `src/entrypoints/machinery/stop_on_pr_close.ts`

Script args: `--number N` (PR number). Maybe also `--outcome` (merged or not) — the notice text differs? Let's think about what notice to post.

Design:
- Read the PR's thread comments (listComments) and determine:
  1. Is there a live claim? claim tag (`atomaton:took`) with no ending after it. Use `runInFlight(repo, number)` with default merged: false? But careful: `runInFlight` with merged false uses `shaped.holder === "agent" || whoseTurn(events) === "agent"`. The second half is "a request or handoff is the newest word". For a merged PR whose thread ends with `ended=handoff` (the old #449 defect) — but with #449 fixed, the post-merge handoff is written on the issue, not the PR. Still, using the event rule would count a merged PR with a handoff ending as in flight — the very #443 defect. Hmm, but here we're on the PR's own `closed` event and we want to stop a run that is actually polling the PR thread. The event rule's "a run is coming" half is bogus for merged PRs (that's #449). But for a non-merged closed PR, a run could genuinely be dispatched... no, a closed PR can't get new runs either after close? Actually a closed unmerged PR can be reopened and dispatched. But right now, at close time, "a request is the newest word" means a run was dispatched to this PR and may be starting — that run polls the PR thread for stop tags. So for a closed PR, a request-outstanding should count for stopping.

The spec says: gate on a live claim (claim with no ending after it), explicitly NOT `runningOn`/`runInFlight(..., {merged: true})`. Using `runInFlight(repo, number)` without the merged option gives claim OR event rule. The instruction says "生きた claim（claim の後に ending が無い）があること" — "a live claim (no ending after the claim)". That's `runInFlight`'s merged:true path: `shaped.holder === "agent"`. Hmm, `holder === "agent"` is set when openClaim is defined, i.e. a claim (`atomaton:took`) with no answering ending. That matches "claim with no ending after it" exactly. So the gate is: `runInFlight(repo, number, { merged: true })`? But the issue says do NOT use `runInFlight(..., { merged: true })`... Wait, re-read:

"1. thread 上に**生きた claim**（claim の後に ending が無い）があること。**`runningOn` / `runInFlight(..., {merged: true})` を使わない** — merged PR を強制的に非稼働とする #449 の設計（`work-tree.ts:95-104`、`thread.ts:441-445`）により、本件のバグ対象そのものが常に false になる。`work-tree.ts:104` が `runInFlight(repo, number, { merged })` と呼んでいるのでオプションは省略可能なはず。`thread.ts:435` 付近を実装読みのうえ、merged オプション無し（または `merged: false`）の呼びで「生 claim の有無」を取る。"

Hmm — that's the parent issue author's guidance, but it's partially mistaken: `runInFlight(..., {merged:true})` returns ONLY `shaped.holder === "agent"`, i.e. exactly the live claim. Whereas `merged:false`/absent returns claim OR event rule. So the parent's stated reason ("merged PR を強制的に非稼働とする設計により、本件のバグ対象そのものが常に false になる") is wrong about merged:true — merged:true passes when there is a live claim, which is exactly what we need (the reviewer that merges its own PR has a live claim).

But wait — does the reviewer that merges its own PR actually have a live claim on the PR thread? Yes: reviewer run started on the PR, wrote `atomaton:took`, and its ending comes after. When it merged mid-run, no ending yet → holder === "agent". So merged:true would be true.

Hmm, but there's a subtlety: for a merged PR whose run already ended, `holder` is "person" → no tag. Good.

But there's a deeper issue: the #449 claim about `runInFlight(merged:true)` — reading `thread.ts:461-475`: `if (options.merged === true) return shaped.holder === "agent";`. So merged:true is strictly narrower. The concern in the handoff was that `runningOn` passes merged and returns running=false for merged PRs... which is only true if there's no claim. Hmm, so the handoff's claim "本件のバグ対象そのものが常に false になる" is imprecise but the recommended gate ("live claim only") is exactly `merged: true` semantics.

I need to decide: which call do I make? The issue's owner-visible spec (comment 4) says the gate should be "a live claim", and to use `runInFlight` without merged option or merged:false. That would also fire on "a request/hand-off is the newest word" — which for a closed PR is... hmm. Consider a merged PR reviewed by `reviewer` where the run already ended with `ended=handoff` written on the PR? With #449's fix, post-merge dispatch is written on the issue, not the PR. But older PRs and other handoffs... Actually an engineer that opens a PR via `create_pr` — create_pr posts an ending comment on... let me check. `create_pr` writes `ended=handoff`/`waiting` on the PR? #449 says "a merged pull request re-invokes the issue it delivers, and until #449 that dispatch was written onto the pull request as ended=handoff". So the post-merge dispatch ended up on the PR.

Given the risk of resurrecting the #443 defect (announcing stops for merged PRs with nothing running), gating on the live claim only is safer AND matches the handoff's stated intent ("生きた claim"). Using `runInFlight(repo, number, { merged: true })` achieves exactly that... but the handoff explicitly says not to use `merged: true`. Hmm, does it say why not in a way that is true? "merged PR を強制的に非稼働とする #449 の設計 ... により、本件のバグ対象そのものが常に false になる" — this is factually wrong, as shown by `thread.ts:473`. But reviewer will judge against the issue spec. The most defensible thing: implement the gate as a *live claim* read explicitly, and explain in the code comment why merged:true's narrowed semantics is exactly the live claim... 

Actually, simplest and clearest: use `openClaimOn`-like reading? `openClaimOn` returns undefined when no openClaim, and includes `claimed` etc. Let me look at what's cleanest:

```ts
const shaped = ... // need access
```

There's no exported function giving "holder" for a merged PR except `runInFlight(repo, n, {merged:true})`. Honestly `runInFlight(repo, number, { merged: true })` is precisely "the thread holds a live claim" and is the least new code. But the handoff (the instruction from the parent agent) forbids it... The instruction's rationale is wrong, though. Which do I follow?

Take the intent: gate = live claim, not the "a run is coming" half. The mechanism options:
1. `runInFlight(repo, n, { merged: true })` — exactly live claim. Comment would explain: `merged: true` asks only the claim half, which is the half a stop can act on.
2. `runInFlight(repo, n)` — live claim OR newest-word event. Wider.

Option 1 satisfies the acceptance criterion "生 claim あり → 投稿 / claim 無し → 投稿なし". Option 2 also satisfies it but additionally fires in the request-outstanding case. The acceptance tests I write define the behaviour; a merged PR with a handoff ending would be a case where option 2 posts a tag to nothing (harmless per design: watcher ignores older tags... but it produces a confusing comment on a merged PR — exactly the #443 defect class).

Hmm, but there IS a real case where a run is coming and not yet claimed: PR closed unmerged while a dispatch to it is outstanding. Rare. The stop wouldn't help since a stop tag posted now would be seen by that run when it starts (a stop newer than its own start? no — the tag is before the run starts, and the watcher ignores tags older than run start). Wait: watcher's `since` is the run's start time; a tag posted before the run started is ignored. So a tag for a not-yet-started run is useless anyway! The only useful tag is for a run that has already started polling, i.e. one that has claimed. 

That settles it decisively: **the gate is a live claim**, and the reason is that a stop tag posted before a run starts is ignored by the watcher (`watch_for_stop.ts:15-19`). So `merged: true`-style claim-only reading is right, and I can state the reason in the code comment (which is stronger than #449's reason). I'll call `runInFlight(repo, number, { merged: true })`? But careful: `merged: true` is the correct *semantics* but the name would be confusing when the PR closed unmerged. The option is documented as "The node is a merged pull request". Passing merged:true for a closed-unmerged PR would be a lie about the node, though it yields the same claim-only reading.

Better: avoid `runInFlight` altogether and read the claim directly from the thread with `openClaimOn`? `openClaimOn` returns `{ask, run, parked, claimed}` when `shaped.openClaim !== undefined` — that's exactly the live claim. But its docstring says "The stop receipt reads this to end a PARK". Using it for a different purpose could be confusing but it's the same question: which claim is open. Hmm, it also does a full `readComments` (paginated list) again — one read.

Actually cleanest: add a tiny exported predicate in `thread.ts`... but the instruction was to keep the change minimal and not touch poller/request_stop. Adding a `liveClaimOn(repo, number)` to `adapters/github/thread.ts` is a small addition, but it must also give the claim's timestamp for the double-tag gate (created_at of the claim comment). Hmm.

I need: (a) whether a live claim exists, (b) the created_at of the claim comment (or of the last claim, to compare against stop tag times), (c) list of STOP_TAG comments with created_at newer than that.

So one read of the thread: `listComments(repo, number)` gives id/body/created_at/user. I can then:
- build `shapedThread` with `readers` to find whether the holder is agent — but shapedThread's output doesn't carry which comment was the claim. However I can compute the live claim myself: walk comments, track the last claim (TOOK_TAG) with no later ending — but that logic is exactly shapedThread's. Duplicating it is what the repo hates.

Alternative: use `openClaimOn(repo, number)` for the boolean (it uses `readComments` internally, throwing on failure) and separately use `listComments` to find the newest claim comment and the stop tags. Two reads of the same thread — meh, but `openClaimOn` also gives `ask`/`run`. Hmm, "one read of the thread" principle.

Hmm, what about: use `listComments` once, then `shapedThread(entries, readers)` — is `shapedThread` exported from domain and `readers` from adapters? Yes both exported. But I'd need to reproduce the claim's timestamp: the claim comment's created_at. If I compute `shapedThread(comments, readers)` to get the boolean and then scan comments backwards for the newest `TOOK_TAG` claim that is prose... 

Alternative simpler rule that the handoff actually specified: find the newest comment carrying `TOOK_TAG` (a claim) — call it the claim. Check whether an ending (`ENDED_TAG`) appears after it. If the newest claim has no ending after it → live. That's a small local walk but it duplicates the domain's logic (e.g. the `waiting` park case: an answered `waiting` ending keeps claim open... which means "live claim" in shapedThread's sense is still open for a parked node; a parked node has no run polling though! `request_stop.ts`'s `parkExit` handles park: `parked && !claimed` → the parked node has no live run, so a stop tag would be posted to nothing... but harmless-ish, and it'd post a confusing comment).

Hmm. Let me just reuse the domain decision properly. What about using both `openClaimOn` and `listComments`? Cost: 2 comment-list reads on a rarely-run job (PR closed). That's fine, but it's a smell.

Better: is there an existing exported helper computing "the shape" plus dated entries? `readRunWatchThread(repo, number)` returns `{dated, entries, events}` — entries carry body/isHuman/quoted/createdAt, and events. But no holder/openClaim. Hmm, `readRunWatchThread` gives events but the claim resolution (closing on answers) isn't exposed.

OK: I'll do one `listComments`, then compute with the domain: `shapedThread(entries, readers).openClaim !== undefined` for the boolean. For the claim's timestamp, I need the claim comment. Let me look at `shapedThread` again — it doesn't expose ids either. But: the claim comment is the newest non-quoted comment in `shaped.comments` that carries `readers.claim(body) !== undefined`... Actually the open claim is the claim of the newest claim-tag comment that has no answering ending. Simple approach: take the *last* comment in `shaped.comments` with a claim tag (`TOOK_TAG.readProse`). If there's an open claim at all, is the last claim the open one? A claim closes when an ending answers it; a later claim supersedes. If the last claim is answered (ending after it with matching answers), then no open claim. So: if `openClaim !== undefined`, the open claim IS the last claim (any later claim would either be the open one or be answered, and if answered then... hmm consider claim A answered then claim B superseded? A claim written while openClaim defined just replaces it). Let me trace shapedThread: for each entry, if claim !== undefined → openClaim = ask (replaces). else if openClaim !== undefined and answered === openClaim and event !== waiting → openClaim = undefined. So the open claim is always the last claim seen. Good — so "last claim comment in shaped.comments" has the same created_at as the open claim.

So plan:

```ts
const comments = listComments(repo, number);  // throws on failure
const entries = comments.map(c => ({ body: c.body ?? "", isHuman: isHumanActor(c.user?.type), quoted: !isHuman && QUOTES_TAG.has(body) }));
const shaped = shapedThread(entries, readers);
if (shaped.openClaim === undefined) → nothing running, return.
```

But entryOf isn't exported. `keptCommentIds` builds entries internally. Hmm, I'd need to build entries myself with QUOTES_TAG + isHumanActor — duplicating entryOf. Is `entryOf` exported? No (function entryOf, not exported). Hmm.

Option: use `openClaimOn(repo, number)` which is exported and returns `{ask, run, parked, claimed}` — and `claimed` tells whether the newest comment is itself a claim. For double-tag gate I need the claim's timestamp. `openClaimOn` doesn't give it.

New idea: the double-tag gate could compare against the **run's claim time**; but another simpler formulation: suppress if there is a STOP_TAG comment newer than *the newest claim comment*. I need the claim comment's timestamp.

What if I use the newest comment with a claim tag from `listComments` directly (raw body scan via `TOOK_TAG.readProse`, skipping quotations — QUOTES_TAG)? A quotation carrying `atomaton:took` in preserved text — the removed comment is a person's comment, which would rarely carry a claim tag; but `guard_comment_during_run` preserves deleted comments. Safer to skip QUOTES_TAG bodies. That's a 3-line scan, using the same tags.

Hmm, but then I'd have two reads again: `openClaimOn` (or shaped) for the boolean + `listComments` for timestamps. 

Let me reconsider: do I really need the exact claim time for the gate? The purpose: don't double-post when the parent-close propagation (`closeSubtreeUnder`) also posted a STOP_TAG, in the same window. Alternative gate: suppress if there is a STOP_TAG comment whose created_at is within a short recent window? No, hacky.

Alternatively: "the newest STOP_TAG comment in the thread is newer than the newest claim comment" → suppress. Both derived from one `listComments` read. If I derive "live claim" from the same raw list (claim tag present, no later ENDED_TAG answering it) I do duplicate the domain rule. How much duplication? The domain rule in shapedThread also handles `waiting` parks and answering by ask id. A simplified version could be wrong in edge cases (park: claim held open by waiting → we'd think not-live → no tag; is that OK? For a parked PR... a parked node has no run; not posting is correct!). Interesting: for a *parked* thread, `shaped.openClaim` is defined (waiting keeps it open) but there's no live run polling. `openClaimOn().parked` tells us. So the "live claim" gate using shapedThread would fire on a parked PR thread, posting a stop tag to nothing. Using my simplified "claim not followed by any ending" would be false there → no post. That seems *better*.

Hmm, but a "claim whose ending hasn't arrived" vs park: the difference is whether the ending is `waiting`. If I use the simplified rule "the newest claim comment is newer than the newest ENDED_TAG comment" → live. For parked: ending (waiting) is newer than claim → not live → no tag. For live run: claim is newest → tag. For a merged PR with old handoff ending and no claim: newest claim? none → not live → no tag. 

And the timestamp I need for the double-tag gate is exactly the newest claim comment's created_at.

That's a simple, defensible rule: **a run is in flight iff the newest claim in the thread is newer than the newest ending**. Wait — is that right in general? An ending after a claim means the claim was answered → turn returned. A claim after the newest ending → the claim is open. Yes, equivalent to openClaim !== undefined AND the newest claim is the one open... careful case: claim A (ask 5), claim B (ask 7) then ending answering 5 — shapedThread: openClaim=5, then claim 7 → openClaim=7, then ending answers 5 ≠ 7 → openClaim stays 7 (live). My rule: newest claim (7) newer than newest ending? The ending is newer than claim 7 → my rule says not live; shapedThread says live. Which is right? A run claimed ask 7 and then an ending answering ask 5 arrived... weird interleaving (two runs). shapedThread's answer (live) is the conservative one. My rule misses it.

Hmm. How likely is that interleaving on a PR thread? Two claims and out-of-order endings: a resumed run answering an older ask while a newer claim is out... possible-ish with `/resume`. This is exactly the kind of "reasonable-looking simplification of a subtle rule" the repo's conventions push against.

Decision: use the domain's answer for the boolean (`openClaimOn(repo, number)` → exported, gives `{..., claimed, parked}`) — actually its semantics: returns defined iff `openClaim` defined. Then "live claim" = `openClaim !== undefined && !parked`? Hmm, `parked` = newest event is "waiting". If parked, the run ended (waiting) → no live run. But careful: `claimed` = newest comment is a claim — i.e. a re-invoked parent claimed a parked ask and is working. In that case, live. So: live = openClaim defined && (!parked || claimed). That's exactly `parkExit`'s negated condition! `parkExit` returns undefined when `!parked || claimed`, i.e. a park end is needed only when parked && !claimed. So: live claim = openClaim defined && (parkExit(openClaim) === undefined) → "not a parked node that nobody holds".

Nice: I can reuse `parkExit`? Importing from `request_stop.ts` would violate "a script may not import another script's ref" — but importing a plain function (not `ref`) from a sibling script... the contract test only checks `ref` imports. But build-dist bundles each script separately; importing a non-ref export from a sibling script would bundle the sibling's code including `main()`?? `import.meta.main` guard prevents main from running, but the sibling's `ref = defineScript(import.meta.url)` would be bundled — harmless since we don't use it, but it does mean duplicated code and `import.meta.url` confusion. It's a smell. The conventions say lib/ subdir isn't bundled as entries; shared code should live in `lib/` or domain/adapters.

Cleanest: put the decision in the domain or adapter layer:
- The gate question "is a run still holding this thread" belongs with `openClaimOn` in `adapters/github/thread.ts` or a domain function.

Let me write in `src/adapters/github/thread.ts`:

```ts
export function liveClaimOn(repo, number): boolean
```
which reads shaped and returns `shaped.openClaim !== undefined && !(parked && !claimed)`. But I also need the claim timestamp for the double-tag gate, which requires dated entries.

Implementation:

```ts
export function stopCoverageOn(repo: string, number: string | number): StopCoverage {
  const shaped = readComments(repo, number);
  const claim = shaped.openClaim;
  if (claim === undefined) return { claimed: false, requested: false };
  const comments = shaped.comments;
  let claimAt = -1;
  for (let i = comments.length - 1; i >= 0; i -= 1) {
    if (readers.claim(comments[i]?.body ?? "")?.ask === claim.ask) { claimAt = i; break; }
  }
  const requested = claimAt >= 0 && comments.slice(claimAt + 1).some((c) => STOP_TAG.hasProse(c.body ?? ""));
  return { claimed: true, requested };
}
```

```ts
/**
 * The receipt a person reads when a pull request closes under a run.
 *
 * The twin of `stopOnCloseNotice`, for the other node kind, and the same rule about
 * what it may claim: it knows the pull request closed, that a run holds it, and that

 * delivered" are both true, and a reader who is told only the first looks for work
 * that is already on the branch. So the merged receipt says the merge happened.
 * It is also the thread a person is most likely to be reading: the merge is what
 * they just did.
 */
export function stopOnPrCloseNotice(number: number, merged: boolean): string {
  if (merged) {
    return [
      "Atomaton: this pull request was merged while an agent was working on it, so the run has been asked to stop.",
      "",
      "Merging does not stop a run by itself — it keeps going until this request reaches it. The run stops after its current step, so it may take a minute.",
      "",
      `What it had done is on the branch #${number} merged into. The run will report here when it has stopped.`,
    ].join("\n");
  }
  return [
    "Atomaton: this pull request was closed while an agent was working on it, so the run has been asked to stop.",
    "",
    "Closing does not stop a run by itself — it keeps going until this request reaches it. The run stops after its current step, so it may take a minute.",
    "",
    `#${number} stays closed, and the run will report here when it has stopped.`,
  ].join("\n");
}
```
